Graded Discussion Board (GDB)
                      ENG-522

Last Date: 13 Dec 2022

Write your own views about the topic. Your
comments should NOT exceed 200-250
words.

Question:

Will linguistics surpass literature in future?
Bulid an argumantative analysis of your own
on this hypothesis. Your response should
be original.

‫کیا مستقبل میں لسانیات ادب سے آگے نکل جائے گی؟ اس‬
‫مفروضے پر اپنا ایک دلیلی تجزیہ بنائیں۔ آپ کا جواب اصل ہونا‬
‫چاہیے۔‬
Solution:

As we know that Linguistics is better for
analyzing languages. Literature is better for
analyzing novels, plays, poetry, and short
stories. They are both different things, although
language is the main element in the two cases.
I would say that if you want to study the artistic,
creative and philosophical side of language,
literature is better. If, on the other hand, you
want a purely scientific approach to language,
linguistics is your best choice. So, we cannot
say that in future linguistics will be better or
literature. You cannot compare apples and
oranges, even if they are fruit. In the same way
you cannot compare linguistics with literature
because they are both equally important for
English language learners.
‫جیسا کہ ہم جانتے ہیں کہ زبانوں کا تجزیہ کرنے کے لیے‬
‫ شاعری اور مختصر کہانیوں کا‬،‫ ڈرامے‬،‫لسانیات بہتر ہے۔ ناول‬
‫تجزیہ کرنے کے لیے ادب بہتر ہے۔ یہ دونوں الگ الگ چیزیں‬
‫ حاالنکہ دونوں صورتوں میں زبان بنیادی عنصر ہے۔ میں‬،‫ہیں‬
‫ تخلیقی اور فلسفیانہ پہلو کا‬،‫کہوں گا کہ اگر آپ زبان کے فنی‬
‫ آپ‬،‫ دوسری طرف‬،‫مطالعہ کرنا چاہتے ہیں تو ادب بہتر ہے۔ اگر‬

‫زبان کے لیے خالص سائنسی نقطہ نظر چاہتے ہیں‪ ،‬تو لسانیات‬
‫آپ کا بہترین انتخاب ہے۔ اس لیے ہم یہ نہیں کہہ سکتے کہ‬
‫مستقبل میں لسانیات بہتر ہوگی یا ادب۔ آپ سیب اور سنتری کا‬
‫موازنہ نہیں کر سکتے‪ ،‬چاہے وہ پھل ہی کیوں نہ ہوں۔ اسی‬
‫طرح آپ لسانیات کا ادب سے موازنہ نہیں کر سکتے کیونکہ یہ‬
‫دونوں انگریزی زبان سیکھنے والوں کے لیے یکساں طور پر‬

Topic-001: Introduction to the Course
If you describe yourself as a linguist to other people outside the discipline, chances are that they
will ask you, ‘How many languages do you speak?’ But if you describe yourself as an Applied
Linguist, they may well go silent completely, wondering what they should say to you next. If you
are lucky, you might get asked, ‘Is that how to teach languages?’ or ‘Is that translation?’ These
questions are not entirely unreasonable, as Applied Linguistics can mean different things to
different people, even among those who would describe themselves as Applied Linguists.

The International Association of Applied Linguistics (AILA) proclaims:
Applied Linguistics is an interdisciplinary field of research and practice dealing with practical
problems of language and communication that can be identified, analysed or solved by applying
available theories, methods or results of Linguistics or by developing new theoretical and
methodological frameworks in linguistics to work on these problems.

The AILA definition is both broad in including, potentially, many different areas such as child
language acquisition, language and communication disorders, multilingualism, language testing,
communication in the workplace, and so on, and narrow in relating Applied Linguistics to
linguistics proper.

What is Language and What is Linguistics?

All linguistics work, whatever specific perspective one may adopt, should ultimately have
something to say about the question, ‘What is this thing called language?’ (Nunan, 2013). Ron
Macaulay (2011) presents ‘Seven Ways of Looking at Language’:
   • language as meaning
   • language as sound
   • language as form
   • language as communication
   • language as identity
   • language as history

                            ©Copyright Virtual University of Pakistan                        Page 2

   • language as symbol
These can be summarized in three rather different conceptualizations of language:
1. as a particular representational system based on the biologically rooted language faculty;
2. as complex and historically evolved patterns of structures;
3. as a social practice and a culturally loaded value system.

The different conceptualizations of language lead to very different methodological perspectives
which together constitute the field of linguistics today. The following are some of the commonly
occurring terms for different branches of linguistics: theoretical linguistics, formal linguistics,
descriptive linguistics, historical linguistics, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, neurolinguistics,
clinical linguistics, cognitive linguistics, forensic linguistics, educational linguistics,
computational linguistics, corpus linguistics and geo-linguistics.
To these we can add sub-branches, i.e., phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics,
pragmatics, dialectology, discourse analysis, critical discourse analysis, stylistics, genre analysis,
second language acquisition and language pathology.

Indeed, the list of sub-braches can go on. It may be useful to look at the differences, but also
similarities, between these different kinds of linguistics in terms of the relationship between the
linguist who does the studying of language and the evidence he or she uses for the study, paying
particular attention to how the evidence is gathered and used in the analysis. The schematization
of the various approaches helps to highlight the commonalities as well as differences between the

Versatile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) made ready for ubiquitous learning. The appearance of new technologies in the mid 21st century also added a social dimension to ICT that took into consideration Networked Learning (NL). Given that language learning is essentially a socio-social encounter, organized learning capabilities have given the possibility to language learning in local area settings. This has rejuvenated the previous frameworks given by CALL. Q. Major concerns of Critical Applied linguistics (1-9)
1. Praxis
It refers to the integration and cooperation of desire and action or theory and
practices. In the traditional view, theory or action is superior and highly respected
than practices or desire. The relationship between the two was unequal. The role of
practice and desire were suppressed with stereotyped vision. But critical applied
linguistic pays due focus on both theory and practice and desire and action. So the
unequal power relation between theory and practice as well as desire and action were
abolished in the case of critical applied linguistics.
2. Criticality
Critical applied linguistics is the most critical discipline in dazzling things from
diverse angles. Criticality is concerned with critical study of social problems. In fact
criticality refers to the logical and examined reflection of things. It is systematic,
critical, objective analysis of facts and problems from various angles. As to the
beliefs of critical applied linguistics, criticality can be taught in classroom situation.
Critical reading, listening, speaking and writing can be taught in language classes.
Thus the concept of criticality in applied linguistics also works with the subject itself.
Criticality is not just a matter of mapping micro applied linguistics in to the macro
social relation, but sustainable critical study of the areas of critical applied linguistics
and all social relations and problems.
3. Critical social study
it refers to the careful examination of social relation. Critical applied linguistics was
based on the assumption that social relation is full of pains and suffrages. So it needs
critical examination. The power imbalance, difference, injustice, hegemony,
suppuration, colonization, subduing and etc. are some of the critical cases that
critical applied linguistic majorly deals with. Thus using critical approaches, critical
applied linguists studies the social problems. The study describes, explains,
expresses and interprets the social problem. Then it calls for the political
interventions. In studying the painful social relation, critical applied linguistics sides
the victimized group in the social relations.

Q: Will Linguistics surpass literature in future? Build an argumentative analysis of your own
on this hypothesis. Your response should be original.

Solution:1

Language plays an important role in everyday aspects of human life. Generally,
English teachers are always concerned about the kind of ideas and information
they impart to their students. In this modern technological age, there are many
ways and resources available to acquire language skills. But language taught and
acquired through literature has its own powerful consequences. Literature is one of
the most in-demand content categories for the English classroom today. It is
confirmed that teaching language through literature promotes effective language
learning. Language through literature expands linguistic knowledge, facilitates
intelligence, stimulates creativity, improves cultural awareness and develops
psychological aspects. Learning a language through literature facilitates
expression, develops reading skills and strategies, and increases fluency and
fluency. Experiencing language through literature encourages dreaming of future

worlds and provides lifelong experience and encourages learners to identify
themselves in different roles.

Literature – Importance and its effectiveness

Literature plays a prominent role in foreign language acquisition and is revived as
an important part of language teaching in view of linguistic and cultural aspects.
Moreover, it has a reinforcing effect in the language class. In English language
teaching, literature is usually used to understand the language. Literature, a part of
the whole humanity, is grappling with universal problems. It paves the way for
acquiring knowledge about multiple structures of a language. Literature serves as a
tool to expand some new methods and techniques in language teaching and
learners can gain more benefits in language learning and proficiency. Literature
helps learners to acquire literary context and facilitate their everyday use and
characters inspire and motivate to overcome various obstacles. It provides their
communication skills of the language.

Solution: 2

The hypothesis that linguistics will surpass literature in the future is both
interesting and complex . linguistics is the study of language , while literature is
the art of storytelling while the two disciplines have some similarities they are
fundamentally different and cannot be compared in a straightforward manner .on
the one hand, the development of technology has allowed for a greater
understanding of language , and this has led to the emergence of new forms of
linguistics and natural language processing . on the other hand , literature has
always been an important part of human culture and will likely remain so in the
future.if the definition of surpass is taken to mean become more important or
influential than then linguistics may indeed surpass literature in the future .as
technology of language and its usage will become ever more important and this
may lead to the emergence of new forms of linguistics that are more influential
than traditional forms of literature.for example the development of artificial
intelligence and natural language processing has allowed for the automation of
many tasks that were once done by humans, and this has led to an increase in the
importance of linguistics .in conclusion , it is difficult to definitively answer

whether linguistics will surpass literature in the future , while technology has
allowed for the emergence of new forms of linguistics , it is unlikely that
linguistics will ever completely replace literature in the future . linguistics will
continue to grow , literature will remain a vital part of our culture and our society
for centuries to come.

ENG522_Glossary

 1. applied linguistics: The application of insights from theoretical linguistics to
    practical matters such as language teaching, remedial linguistic therapy,
    language planning or whatever.
 2. arbitrariness: An essential notion in structural linguistics which denies any
    necessary relationship between linguistic signs and their referents, e.g. objects
    in the outside world.
 3. areas of linguistics: Any of a number of areas of study in which linguistic
    insights have been brought to bear, for instance sociolinguistics in which
    scholars study society and the way language is used in it. Other examples are
    psycholinguistics which is concerned with the psychological and linguistic
    development of the child.
 4. Chronology: Content may be sequenced according to the order in which
    events occur in the real world. For example, in a writing course the
    organization might be based on the sequence writers are assumed to employ
    when composing: (1) brainstorming; (2) drafting; (3) revising; (4) editing. In
    a proficiency course, skills might be sequenced according to the sequence in
    which they are nor-mally acquired: (1) listening; (2) speaking; (3) reading; (4)
    writing.
 5. competence: According to Chomsky in his Aspects of the theory of syntax
    (1965) this is the abstract ability of an individual to speak the language which
    he/she has learned as native language in his/her childhood. The competence
    of a speaker is unaffected by such factors as nervousness, temporary loss of
    memory, speech errors, etc. These latter phenomena are entirely within the
    domain of performance which refers to the process of applying one's
    competence in the act of speaking. Bear in mind that competence also refers

By ASFAND YARR

                            ENG522_Glossary

    to the ability to judge if a sentence is grammatically well-formed; it is an
    unconscious ability.
 6. context: A term referring to the environment in which an element (sound,
    word, phrase) occurs. The context may determine what elements may be
    present, in which case one says that there are 'co-occurrence restrictions' for
    instance 1) /r/ may not occur after /s/ in a syllable in English, e.g. */sri:n/ is
    not phonotactically permissible in English; 2) the progressive form cannot
    occur with stative verbs, e.g. We are knowing German is not well-formed in
    English.
 7. contrast: A difference between two linguistic items which can be exploited
    systematically. The distinction between the two forms arises from the fact that
    these can occupy one and the same slot in a syntagm, i.e. they alternate
    paradigmatically, e.g. the different inflectional forms of verbs contrast in both
    English and German. Forms which contrast are called distinctive. This can
    apply to sounds as well, for instance /p/ and /b/ contrast in English as minimal
    pairs such as pin /p?n/ : bin/b?n/ show.
 8. convention: An agreement, usually reached unconsciously by speakers in a
    community, that relationships are to apply between linguistic items, between
    these and the outside world or to apply in the use of rules in the grammar of
    their language.
 9. Course Planning: A number of different levels of planning and development
    are involved in developing a course or set of instructional materials based on
    the aims and objectives that have been established for a language program.
 10.      creativity: An accepted feature of human language — deriving from
    the phenomenon of sentence generation — which accounts for speakers'

By ASFAND YARR

                           ENG522_Glossary

   ability to produce and to understand a theoretically infinite number of
   sentences.
 11.       descriptive: An approach to linguistics which is concerned with saying
   what language is like and not what it should be like (prescriptivism).
 12.       diachronic: Refers to language viewed over time and contrasts with
   synchronic which refers to a point in time. This is one of the major structural
   distinctions introduced by Saussure and which is used to characterise types of
   linguistic investigation.
 13.       displacement: One of the key characteristics of human language which
   enables it to refer to situations which are not here and now, e.g. I studied
   linguistics in London when I was in my twenties.
 14.       duality of patterning: A structural principle of human language
   whereby larger units consist of smaller building blocks, the number of such
   blocks being limited but the combinations being almost infinite. For instance
   all words consist of combinations of a limited number of sounds, say about 40
   in either English or German. Equally all sentences consist of structures from
   a small set with different words occupying different points in the structures
   allowing for virtually unlimited variety.
 15.       economy: A principle of linguistic analysis which demands that rules
   and units are to be kept to a minimum, i.e. every postulated rule or unit must
   be justified linguistically by capturing a generalisation about the language
   being analysed, if not about all languages.
 16.       Effective Teaching: Quality teaching is achieved not only as a
   consequence of how well teachers teach but through creating contexts and
   good.

                          ENG522_Glossary

 17.     extralinguistic: Any phenomenon which lies outside of language. An
   extralinguistic reason for a linguistic feature would be one which is not to be
   found in the language itself.
 18.     figurative: Any use of a word in a non-literal sense, e.g. at the foot of
   the mountain where foot is employed figuratively to indicate the bottom of
   the mountain. Figurative usage is the source of the second meaning of
   polysemous words.
 19.     formalist: An adjective referring to linguistic analyses which lay
   emphasis on relatively abstract conceptions of language structure.

    necessary relationship between linguistic signs and their referents, e.g. objects
    in the outside world.
 3. areas of linguistics: Any of a number of areas of study in which linguistic
    insights have been brought to bear, for instance sociolinguistics in which
    scholars study society and the way language is used in it. Other examples are
    psycholinguistics which is concerned with the psychological and linguistic
    development of the child.
 4. Chronology: Content may be sequenced according to the order in which
    events occur in the real world. For example, in a writing course the
    organization might be based on the sequence writers are assumed to employ
    when composing: (1) brainstorming; (2) drafting; (3) revising; (4) editing. In
    a proficiency course, skills might be sequenced according to the sequence in
    which they are nor-mally acquired: (1) listening; (2) speaking; (3) reading; (4)
    writing.
 5. competence: According to Chomsky in his Aspects of the theory of syntax
    (1965) this is the abstract ability of an individual to speak the language which
    he/she has learned as native language in his/her childhood. The competence
    of a speaker is unaffected by such factors as nervousness, temporary loss of
    memory, speech errors, etc. These latter phenomena are entirely within the
    domain of performance which refers to the process of applying one's
    competence in the act of speaking. Bear in mind that competence also refers

By ASFAND YARR

                            ENG522_Glossary

    to the ability to judge if a sentence is grammatically well-formed; it is an
    unconscious ability.
 6. context: A term referring to the environment in which an element (sound,
    word, phrase) occurs. The context may determine what elements may be
    present, in which case one says that there are 'co-occurrence restrictions' for
    instance 1) /r/ may not occur after /s/ in a syllable in English, e.g. */sri:n/ is
    not phonotactically permissible in English; 2) the progressive form cannot
    occur with stative verbs, e.g. We are knowing German is not well-formed in
    English.
 7. contrast: A difference between two linguistic items which can be exploited
    systematically. The distinction between the two forms arises from the fact that
    these can occupy one and the same slot in a syntagm, i.e. they alternate
    paradigmatically, e.g. the different inflectional forms of verbs contrast in both
    English and German. Forms which contrast are called distinctive. This can
    apply to sounds as well, for instance /p/ and /b/ contrast in English as minimal
    pairs such as pin /p?n/ : bin/b?n/ show.
 8. convention: An agreement, usually reached unconsciously by speakers in a
    community, that relationships are to apply between linguistic items, between
    these and the outside world or to apply in the use of rules in the grammar of
    their language.
 9. Course Planning: A number of different levels of planning and development
    are involved in developing a course or set of instructional materials based on
    the aims and objectives that have been established for a language program.
 10.      creativity: An accepted feature of human language — deriving from
    the phenomenon of sentence generation — which accounts for speakers'

By ASFAND YARR

                           ENG522_Glossary

   ability to produce and to understand a theoretically infinite number of
   sentences.
 11.       descriptive: An approach to linguistics which is concerned with saying
   what language is like and not what it should be like (prescriptivism).
 12.       diachronic: Refers to language viewed over time and contrasts with
   synchronic which refers to a point in time. This is one of the major structural
   distinctions introduced by Saussure and which is used to characterise types of
   linguistic investigation.
 13.       displacement: One of the key characteristics of human language which
   enables it to refer to situations which are not here and now, e.g. I studied
   linguistics in London when I was in my twenties.
 14.       duality of patterning: A structural principle of human language
   whereby larger units consist of smaller building blocks, the number of such
   blocks being limited but the combinations being almost infinite. For instance
   all words consist of combinations of a limited number of sounds, say about 40
   in either English or German. Equally all sentences consist of structures from
   a small set with different words occupying different points in the structures
   allowing for virtually unlimited variety.
 15.       economy: A principle of linguistic analysis which demands that rules
   and units are to be kept to a minimum, i.e. every postulated rule or unit must
   be justified linguistically by capturing a generalisation about the language
   being analysed, if not about all languages.
 16.       Effective Teaching: Quality teaching is achieved not only as a
   consequence of how well teachers teach but through creating contexts and
   good.

By ASFAND YARR

                          ENG522_Glossary

 17.     extralinguistic: Any phenomenon which lies outside of language. An
   extralinguistic reason for a linguistic feature would be one which is not to be
   found in the language itself.
 18.     figurative: Any use of a word in a non-literal sense, e.g. at the foot of
   the mountain where foot is employed figuratively to indicate the bottom of
   the mountain. Figurative usage is the source of the second meaning of
   polysemous words.
 19.     formalist: An adjective referring to linguistic analyses which lay
   emphasis on relatively abstract conceptions of language structure.

Topic-001: Introduction to the Course
If you describe yourself as a linguist to other people outside the discipline, chances are that they
will ask you, ‘How many languages do you speak?’ But if you describe yourself as an Applied
Linguist, they may well go silent completely, wondering what they should say to you next. If you
are lucky, you might get asked, ‘Is that how to teach languages?’ or ‘Is that translation?’ These
questions are not entirely unreasonable, as Applied Linguistics can mean different things to
different people, even among those who would describe themselves as Applied Linguists.

The International Association of Applied Linguistics (AILA) proclaims:
Applied Linguistics is an interdisciplinary field of research and practice dealing with practical
problems of language and communication that can be identified, analysed or solved by applying
available theories, methods or results of Linguistics or by developing new theoretical and
methodological frameworks in linguistics to work on these problems.

The AILA definition is both broad in including, potentially, many different areas such as child
language acquisition, language and communication disorders, multilingualism, language testing,
communication in the workplace, and so on, and narrow in relating Applied Linguistics to
linguistics proper.

What is Language and What is Linguistics?

All linguistics work, whatever specific perspective one may adopt, should ultimately have
something to say about the question, ‘What is this thing called language?’ (Nunan, 2013). Ron
Macaulay (2011) presents ‘Seven Ways of Looking at Language’:
   • language as meaning
   • language as sound
   • language as form
   • language as communication
   • language as identity
   • language as history

                            ©Copyright Virtual University of Pakistan                        Page 2

   • language as symbol
These can be summarized in three rather different conceptualizations of language:
1. as a particular representational system based on the biologically rooted language faculty;
2. as complex and historically evolved patterns of structures;
3. as a social practice and a culturally loaded value system.

The different conceptualizations of language lead to very different methodological perspectives
which together constitute the field of linguistics today. The following are some of the commonly
occurring terms for different branches of linguistics: theoretical linguistics, formal linguistics,
descriptive linguistics, historical linguistics, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, neurolinguistics,
clinical linguistics, cognitive linguistics, forensic linguistics, educational linguistics,
computational linguistics, corpus linguistics and geo-linguistics.
To these we can add sub-branches, i.e., phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics,
pragmatics, dialectology, discourse analysis, critical discourse analysis, stylistics, genre analysis,
second language acquisition and language pathology.

Indeed, the list of sub-braches can go on. It may be useful to look at the differences, but also
similarities, between these different kinds of linguistics in terms of the relationship between the
linguist who does the studying of language and the evidence he or she uses for the study, paying
particular attention to how the evidence is gathered and used in the analysis. The schematization
of the various approaches helps to highlight the commonalities as well as differences between the

ENG522
Language in Society Topics

   1. Language in Society: This looks at how language is used in social contexts. It studies
      how language reflects social roles, relationships, and power, and how people use
      language to interact in different social settings.

ICT and Language Teaching

   2. ICT and Language Teaching: ICT (Information and Communication Technology)
      refers to using technology, like computers, smartphones, and the internet, to support
      language teaching. It involves using online resources, apps, and tools to help students
      learn languages more effectively.

Language and Identity

   3. Language and Identity: This explores how the language we speak shapes our identity,
      and how the language we use can influence how we are perceived by others. Our choice
      of language can reflect our culture, background, or social group.

Language, Thought, and Culture

   4. Language, Thought, and Culture: This refers to the idea that the language we speak can
      influence the way we think and perceive the world. Language and culture are closely
      connected because language is a tool for expressing cultural values, beliefs, and thoughts.

Language and Communication

   5. Language and Communication: Communication is how we share ideas, information, or
      feelings with others, and language is one of the main tools we use for communication.
      This term focuses on the ways in which language helps us connect with others, whether
      through speaking, writing, or gestures.

Psycholinguistics, Sociolinguistics, and Educational Aspects

   6. Psycholinguistics: This field studies how people understand, produce, and acquire
      language in their minds. It looks at how language is processed in the brain, including how
      we understand and use words and sentences.

   7. Sociolinguistics: This looks at the relationship between language and society. It studies
      how language varies between different social groups, regions, or communities, and how
      language can reflect things like social status, identity, and culture.
   8. Educational Aspects: This refers to how language is taught and learned in educational
      settings, considering how students acquire language skills and how language impacts
      learning.

Language Planning and Language Policy (LPP)

   9. Language Planning and Language Policy (LPP): Language planning refers to efforts
      by governments or institutions to manage and regulate language use in a society, such as
      deciding which languages are taught in schools or used in government. Language policy
      is the set of rules or guidelines for how languages should be used in various areas of
      society.

Critical Applied Linguistics

   10. Critical Applied Linguistics: This approach to language studies looks at how language
       can be used to challenge power structures in society. It examines the social, political, and
       cultural implications of language use, focusing on issues like inequality, discrimination,
       and the role of language in shaping societal norms.

ENG522
Introducing Applied Linguistics

Applied linguistics is the interdisciplinary field that bridges theoretical linguistics with real-
world language issues. It focuses on solving practical problems related to language in diverse
areas such as education, communication, and sociocultural contexts. Unlike theoretical
linguistics, which examines the structure and function of language abstractly, applied linguistics
deals with how language is used, taught, and learned in specific environments. Key areas include
language acquisition, bilingualism, sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, and language policy. For
instance, applied linguists explore how children acquire their first language or how adults learn a
second language, providing insights into curriculum development, language teaching, and
policy-making.

Language Development

Language development refers to the process by which humans acquire, process, and use
language. This process begins in early childhood and continues throughout life as individuals are
exposed to new linguistic contexts. Key milestones include phonological (sound), syntactic
(sentence structure), semantic (meaning), and pragmatic (social use of language) development.
Theories explaining language development include Noam Chomsky’s Universal Grammar,
which suggests that humans are biologically predisposed to learn language, and B.F. Skinner’s
Behaviorism, emphasizing the role of environment and reinforcement. Language development is
also influenced by factors such as cognitive growth, social interaction, and cultural exposure, and
its study informs both first-language acquisition in children and second-language acquisition in
learners of all ages.

Teaching and Learning Language: Approaches, Methods, and Practices

Language teaching methodologies have evolved significantly, reflecting shifts in pedagogical
theory and research. Approaches such as the Grammar-Translation Method focus on reading
and writing, emphasizing grammar rules and vocabulary memorization. In contrast, the Direct
Method prioritizes speaking and listening through immersive practices without translation. The
Audio-Lingual Method, influenced by behaviorist psychology, uses repetition and drills to
instill language habits. More recently, the Communicative Language Teaching (CLT)
approach has gained prominence, emphasizing interaction and practical communication.
Practices within these methodologies vary, from task-based learning to flipped classrooms, and

they are adapted based on learner needs, age, cultural contexts, and technological resources.
These approaches guide curriculum design and teaching strategies to achieve effective language
acquisition.

Error Analysis: Nature of Errors and Mistakes

Error analysis examines the types and causes of errors made by language learners to better
understand the learning process and inform teaching methods. Errors occur due to gaps in a
learner's knowledge of the target language, while mistakes are typically performance slips caused
by fatigue or distraction. Pioneered by linguist Corder in the 1960s, error analysis focuses on
understanding interlanguage—learners’ evolving language systems that combine elements of
their first language with the target language. Errors are often categorized as grammatical (e.g.,
incorrect verb tense), phonological (e.g., mispronunciations), or pragmatic (e.g., inappropriate
use of politeness). Identifying patterns of errors helps teachers address specific linguistic
challenges and adapt instruction to meet learner needs.

Syllabus Designing

Syllabus design is the process of planning and organizing the content, objectives, and structure of
a language course. It serves as a roadmap for teachers and learners, outlining what will be taught
and how. Common types of syllabi include grammatical syllabi, which focus on linguistic
structures, and functional-notional syllabi, which emphasize language functions and
communication. Modern syllabi often adopt a task-based or content-based approach,
integrating real-world tasks or subject matter into the curriculum. Effective syllabus design
considers learner needs, teaching contexts, available resources, and assessment criteria. It also
incorporates flexibility to accommodate varying proficiency levels and learning styles, ensuring
that language instruction remains relevant and engaging.

Language Assessment: Testing and Evaluation

Language assessment involves measuring learners’ proficiency, progress, or achievements in a
target language. This includes formal tests, informal evaluations, and performance-based tasks.
Key types of language tests include diagnostic tests (identifying strengths and weaknesses),
formative assessments (ongoing feedback during learning), and summative assessments
(evaluating overall achievement at the end of a course). Effective language assessment adheres to
principles of validity (measuring what it claims to measure), reliability (producing consistent
results), and fairness. Modern approaches emphasize communicative competence, incorporating
tasks that simulate real-life language use. Evaluation methods, such as rubrics and portfolios,
provide comprehensive insights into learner performance, guiding both instruction and
curriculum improvements.

         and meet external requirements such as industry standards or academic
         prerequisites. This learner-centered approach ensures that the syllabus is
         relevant, engaging, and beneficial to the students.
Q. Two rules of Traditional grammar
   1.    Subject-Verb Agreement: This rule states that the verb must agree in
         number (singular or plural) with its subject. For example, in the sentence
         "The cat (singular subject) runs (singular verb) fast," the singular verb
         "runs" agrees with the singular subject "cat." Conversely, in "The cats
         (plural subject) run (plural verb) fast," the plural verb "run" agrees with the
         plural subject "cats."
   2.    Proper Use of Tenses: Traditional grammar requires the correct use of
         verb tenses to indicate the time of action or state of being. This includes
         maintaining consistency within a sentence or related sentences. For
         instance, in the sentence "She was studying when he called," the past
         continuous tense "was studying" is used to show an ongoing action in the
         past, and the simple past tense "called" is used to show an action that
         occurred at a specific time in the past. Proper tense use ensures clarity and
         temporal coherence in communication.

Q. Two kinds of achievements test
   • Final achievement test
   • Progress achievement test
Q. Telegraphic stage
A child stays at the telegraphic stage for about half a year followed by a time when
they constantly acquire more complex grammar into their speech along with a
remarkable growth of vocabulary.
This happens when a child’s utterances become longer and more complex, usually
around the time they reach two years of age. It is called the telegraphic stage because
children will not yet have acquired bound morphemes in their speech, making their
utterances resemble telegrams.
The child’s abilities at syntactic order are remarkably good at the telegraphic stage.

Q. Grammar translation method
Methods and approaches may differ in their theoretical background, their focus and
goals, views on teacher and learner roles, typical techniques and forms of interaction,
attitude to errors and use of mother tongue, role of instructional materials, etc. Each
of them has its own strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT).
Q. Validity test
Validity is also an important term related to tests and it is defined as the extent to
which the instrument measures what it purports to measure. For example, in a test
that is used to test students’ listening ability, grammar should not be scored to
preserve validity.
Q. Types of Validity

   • Face validity

Q 1: Differentiate between Sociolinguistics and Sociology of Language? (Imp)
Sociolinguistics differs from sociology of language
    Sociolinguistics:
     It is the effect of the society on the language
    Sociology of language:
      It focuses on effect of language on society
Q 2: Differentiate between sex and gender? (Imp)
    Sex:
     It is refers to the different biological and physiological characteristics of
     males and females such as chromosomes and hormones etc.
    Gender:
     It is refers to the socially and culturally constructed characteristics of
     women and men such as norms etc
Q 3: Define gender roles and gender stereotypes?
    Gender roles:
     These are asks and activities a culture assigns to the sexes – expected ways
     of behaving based on society‟s definition of masculine and feminine.
    Gender stereotypes:
      Oversimplified but strongly held ideas of the characteristics of men and
     women. Gender stratification: An unequal distribution of rewards (socially

1|P ag e

      valued resources, power, prestige, and personal freedom) between men and
      women
Q 4: Define gender stratification and gender ideology?
    Gender stratification:
     An unequal distribution of rewards (socially valued resources, power,
     prestige, and personal freedom) between men and women
    Gender ideology:
     A system of thoughts and values that legitimizes sex roles, statuses and
     customary behavior. Gender is an important dimension of social inequality.
Q5) Define social hierarchy and genderlects?
    Social hierarchy:
      It is a division in society where all members are hierarchically ranked
     according to gender
    Genderlects:
      it means Men often use socially disfavored variants of sociolinguistic
     variables while women tend to avoid these in favor of socially more favored
     variants.
Q6) Define the term intonation?
Intonation refers to the combination of rhythm, volume and pitch overlaying entire
utterances. In general women use wider range of pitches and more rapid shift in
volume and velocity. In other words women talk melodically and faster than men
who are more monotone and slower.
Q7) Define affective tags and enlist its types?
Affective tags:
These tags "are used not to signal uncertainty on the part of the speaker, but to
indicate concern for the addressee" For example Open the door for me, could you?
Affective tags are further subdivided into two kinds
    Softeners
    Facilitative tags
Q8) The use of words can be seen in three ways enlist them?

2|P ag e

    Manslaughter
    Legislature
    Prosecution Attorney
Q 9: Enlist modes of meaning?
    Written meaning
    Spoken ( oral) meaning
    Visual meaning
    Audio meaning
    Spatial meaning
    Gestural meaning
Q10) Enlist types of multimodal texts? (Imp)
There are three types of multimodal texts which are following;
    Paper based multimodal texts
    Live multimodal texts
    Digital multimodal texts
Q11) Enlist the names of three types of meaning organized as sub-stands?
(Imp)
    Expressing and developing ideas
    Interacting and relating with others
    Text structure and organization
Q12) Define Autonomous and Blended learning?
    Autonomous learning:
     Autonomous learning consists in the need to make the teaching more
     effective and to exploit a student‟s potential and particularly his/ her
     creativity . To be autonomous, learners need to be able to have some choice
     in what, where, when and how to study.
    Blended learning:
     There is a prime focus on the fields of knowledge in which citizens acquire
     the skills and
     knowledge necessary for effective communication, i.e. on the teaching of
     foreign languages and ICT.

3|P ag e

Q13) Enlist types of CALL activities only names? (Imp)
    Multiple-choice & true/false quizzes
    Gap-filling exercise/cloze
    Matching
    Re-ordering/sequencing
    Crossword puzzles
    Games
    Simulations
    Writing & word-processing
    Concordancing
    Web quests/searching
    Web publishing
    Online communication (synchronous and asynchronous)
Q14) Write the Roles of the computer in language learning and teaching?
(Imp)
The following roles can be seen:
   1) Computer as tutor for language drills or skill practice
   2) Computer as a tool for writing, presenting, and researching
   3) Computer as a medium of global communication

Q15) What are the advantages of teaching learning? (Imp)
Here are some of the advantages of teaching learning
   1) Self-paced or learner-centered
   2) An active process CALL material is consistent within individual courses.
   3) Getting to know the students' individual
   4) Problems and successes with the learning material.
   5) Working with a group of disciplined students.
   6) Focusing on the important or more difficult material during class time or
      tutoring
      Sessions
Q16) Instrumental competence requires mastering skills in five areas write
those areas?

4|P ag e

   1) Efficient use of CAT (Computer Aided Translation) tools (including
      “general” and
      “specialised” translation technologies),
   2) Ability to use the Internet and communication technologies,
   3) Efficient information mining and terminology management skills,
   4) Document production skills,
   5) Ability to use documentation resources
Q17) Explain Giddens’s theory of structuration? (Imp)
    This theory was given by Anthony Gidden in 1984 so this is known as
     theory of structuration or Gidden‟s theory of structuration
    According to Giddens, individual agency is a semiotic activity, a social
     construction, „something that has to be routinely created and sustained in the
     reflexive activities of the individual‟
    In our locally occasioned social actions, we, as individual agents, shape and
     at the same time are given shape by what Giddens refers to as social
     structures

The International Association of Applied Linguistics (AILA) proclaims:
Applied Linguistics is an interdisciplinary field of research and practice dealing with practical
problems of language and communication that can be identified, analyzed or solved by applying
available theories, methods or results of Linguistics or by developing new theoretical and
methodological frameworks in linguistics to work on these problems.
AILA proclaims, with ‘practical problems of language and communication’, the term
‘problem’ does raise issues of its own.
 Ron Macaulay (2011) presents ‘Seven Ways of Looking at Language’:
    • language as meaning
    • language as sound
    • language as form
    • language as communication
    • language as identity
    • language as history
    • language as symbol
These can be summarized in three rather different conceptualizations of language:
1. as a particular representational system based on the biologically rooted language
faculty;
2. as complex and historically evolved patterns of structures;
3. as a social practice and a culturally loaded value system.
Ben Rampton (1997, p. 14) described Applied Linguistics as ‘an open field of interest in
language’, while David Block (2009) called it ‘an amalgam of research interests’.
The Need and Scope of Applied Linguistics

Applied linguistics is a theoretical term that covers interdisciplinary domain in linguistics to
solve real world problems in the use of language in various contexts such as translation, literacy,
language education and teaching, lexicography, and others which belong to the application of
language. The scope of applied linguistics can be summarized as follows:
1. Language and Teaching: This scope covers the approaches and methods which are used
    in teaching second language.
2. Language and Society: This scope is also called sociolinguistics which studies the
    relationship between the society and language. It answers some questions emerge in the
    use of language in society.

3. Language and Education/Learning: There are some activities involve in this scope.
   They are 1st language education, additional language education, clinical linguistics, and
   language testing.
4. Language, Work, and Law: It covers the studies of workplace communication,
   language planning, and forensic linguistics.
5. Language, Information, and Effect: The other studies such as literary stylistics, CDA
   (Critical Discourse Analysis), translation and interpretation, and information design
   belong to this scope.
Linguistics and Applied Linguistics: A Difficult Relationship

Linguistics and applied linguistics a difficult relationship… Linguistics: is the academic
discipline concerned with the study of language in general. In some degree is bound to
represent an abstract idealization of language. One particularly influential type of
idealization is that used in the generative linguistics by Noam Chomsky. The
representation of language in the mind (competence) the way in which people use
language in everyday life (performance)
In Functional linguistics the concern is with language as a means of communication, and
how people actually use their language. Corpus linguistics looks for the frequencies and
combinations in words that are not usually revealed by intuition.
TOPIC: 5
One important source of that enrichment has been the journal
Language Learning, published from the University of Michigan.
Corder (1973) was well aware that in limiting the coverage of applied linguistics to language
teaching he was open to criticism.
Definitions of Applied Linguistics
“the theoretical and empirical investigation of real-world problems in which language is a central
issue” (Brumfit,

•   “the focus of applied linguistics is on trying to resolve language-based problems that
    people encounter in the real world, whether they be learners, teachers, supervisors,
    academics, lawyers, service providers, those who need social services, test takers,
    policy developers, dictionary makers, translators, or a whole range of business
    clients” (Grabe, 2002, p. 9).
•   Kaplan suggests that applied linguists “are likely to move toward the analysis of new
    data, rather than continue to argue new theory” (Kaplan, 2002, p. 514).
•   “the term ‘applied linguistics’ raises fundamental difficulties, if for no other reason
    than that it is difficult to decide on what counts as ‘linguistics’. Given these
    difficulties within linguistics proper, it is perhaps unfair to expect clean solutions and
    clear delimitations for defining applied linguistics’ ” (Kaplan & Grabe, 2000, pp. 5–
    6).

History of Linguistics:
Angelis summarizes this history as follows:
• Applied Linguistics in North America does have identifiable roots in linguistics.

The British Association of Applied Linguistics (BAAL) was formally established in
1967, with the following aims: “the advancement of education by fostering and
promoting, by any lawful charitable means, the study of language use, language
acquisition and language teaching and the fostering of inter-disciplinary collaboration in
this study” (BAAL)
Methodological Consideration:
Applied Linguistics is a methodology in itself, because it is concerned with real-world problems
in which language plays a central role.
    In general terms, quantitative methodology aims to uncover facts and truths in an objective
    way by delineating patterns or structures, whereas qualitative methodology attempts to
    interpret meanings of and relationships between objects in context.
    Whatever methodology you choose to adopt, there are certain steps you need to take in
    conducting a research project. These typically include:
   1. defining the research question or questions
   2. collecting evidence
   3. analysing and presenting findings

    Defining the research question
    Defining the research question is a crucial first step. The question has to be researchable,
    which means that
   1. there are potentially different answers to it

Introduction to Applied Linguistics
      o Definition: Applied Linguistics is the study of how language is used
        in real-world contexts and how it impacts communication, language
        teaching, and language learning.
      o Purpose: It helps bridge the gap between theoretical linguistics
        (which studies language structure) and practical language use.
      o Areas of Focus: Applied Linguistics covers topics such as language
        acquisition, language teaching methodologies, language
        assessment, and sociolinguistics.
      o Example: Research on effective language teaching methods or
        analyzing language errors in second language learners falls under
        applied linguistics.
Language Development
      o Definition: Language development refers to the process by which
        individuals acquire and improve their language skills over time.
      o Stages: It starts from infancy (babbling) and progresses through
        childhood (vocabulary growth, grammar acquisition) into
        adulthood.
      o Factors: Environmental exposure, interaction, and cognitive
        development play crucial roles in language development.
      o Importance: Understanding language development helps educators
        tailor teaching methods to learners' needs.
Teaching and Learning Language: Approaches, Methods and Practices
      o Approaches: These are overarching principles guiding language
        teaching. Examples include communicative approach, task-based
        learning, and content-based instruction.

      o Methods: Specific techniques used in the classroom, such as role-
         playing, pair work, or using multimedia resources.
      o Practices: Actual implementation of methods during language
         lessons.
      o Effective Teaching: Combining various approaches, methods, and
         practices to create engaging and learner-centered language classes.
Error Analysis: Nature of Errors and Mistakes
      o Error vs. Mistake: Errors are systematic deviations from language
         rules, while mistakes are unintentional slips (e.g., due to
         forgetfulness).
      o Importance: Analyzing errors helps teachers understand learners'
         language development and tailor instruction accordingly.
      o Example: Identifying common errors made by English learners
         (e.g., verb tense errors) and addressing them in teaching.
Syllabus Designing
   o Purpose: Creating a syllabus involves planning the content, structure,
      and assessment methods for a course.
   o Components: A syllabus typically includes basic information
      (instructor details, course title), course description, learning objectives,
      assessment criteria, and a schedule.
   o Adaptability: Syllabi should be flexible to accommodate learners'
      needs and unexpected events.
   o Effective Syllabus: Balancing clarity, expectations, and engagement to
      enhance student learning.
Language Assessment: Testing and Evaluation
      o Purpose: Assessing language proficiency, progress, and
         achievement.
      o Types: Includes formative assessments (during learning) and
         summative assessments (end-of-course evaluations).
      o Methods: Tests, quizzes, oral interviews, portfolios, and self-
         assessment.
      o Validity and Reliability: Ensuring assessments measure what they
         intend to and yield consistent results.

        o Ethical Considerations: Fairness, transparency, and minimizing
          bias in assessment practices.

Lesson 01
                Introduction to Applied Linguistics

Introduction to Applied Linguistics
What is the definition of Applied Linguistics according to the International
Association of Applied Linguistics (AILA)?
AILA defines Applied Linguistics as an interdisciplinary field that deals with
practical language and communication problems using linguistic theories,
methods, and results, or by developing new theoretical and methodological
frameworks.
What are some areas that Applied Linguistics can encompass, as mentioned in
the AILA definition?
Applied Linguistics can include areas such as child language acquisition, language
and communication disorders, multilingualism, language testing, communication
in the workplace, and more.
What are the seven different ways of looking at language, as presented by Ron
Macaulay?
The seven ways of looking at language are language as meaning, sound, form,
communication, identity, history, and symbol.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           1

How does the conceptualization of language affect the methodological
perspectives in linguistics?
Different conceptualizations of language lead to various methodological
perspectives in linguistics, influencing how linguists gather and analyze evidence.
This diversity characterizes the different branches and sub-branches of linguistics.
What distinguishes the first schematized approach to linguistics (Figure 1.1)
from the second approach (Figure 1.2)?
The first approach relies on the linguist's intuition and knowledge of the language
without separately collected data. In contrast, the second approach uses a
database for analysis, which can be derived from the language users.
What are the key implications for Applied Linguists discussed in the text?
       The key implications for Applied Linguists are:
    1. Applied Linguists need to be multidisciplinary and have knowledge in
       various areas.
    2. Applied Linguists act as consultants, providing advice and interpretation but
       leaving the final decision to the client.
    3. Describing language, on its own, is not considered Applied Linguistics unless
       it contributes to problem-solving.
How does Applied Linguistics differ from descriptive linguistics?
Applied Linguistics focuses on solving real-world language problems, while
descriptive linguistics primarily concerns the analysis and description of language
without an immediate problem-solving objective.
What is the unique selling point of Applied Linguistics that distinguishes it from
other disciplines, according to the text?
The unique selling point of Applied Linguistics is its central focus on language. It
distinguishes itself from other disciplines by dealing with language-related
problems and research that are relevant to language practice.
The Black English Trial in Ann Arbor (Labov, 1982)
What is the significance of the Ann Arbor case in 1977?
The Ann Arbor case was significant as it raised questions about the educational
failure of black children in the United States, particularly related to their language
and the so-called "restricted code."
Why did linguists become involved in the Ann Arbor case?
Linguists became involved to provide testimony and evidence about the linguistic
facts and challenges faced by black children, as their language was central to the
case.
What linguistic features characterized Black English Vernacular (BEV)?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                              2

BEV included features such as the zero form of the possessive, habitual be,
absence of 3rd person singular "s," and more.
Labov's Principles and the Trial Outcome
What principles did Labov enunciate regarding social action?
Labov outlined principles like "error correction" and "obligation" for scientists
involved in social action, emphasizing the responsibility to share important data
with the public.
Why was it essential for linguists to present a united front during the trial?
Linguists needed to present a united front to ensure a consensus on linguistic
issues, which was crucial for the trial's success.
The Role of Applied Linguists and Career Opportunities
What distinguishes Applied Linguistics as a methodology?
Applied Linguistics focuses on real-world language problems, making it a
methodology that emphasizes practical problem-solving.
What are some potential career opportunities for graduates with a background
in Applied Linguistics?
Career opportunities include roles such as language teachers, language education
experts, speech pathologists, translators/interpreters, and more.
Defining Research Questions and Literature Review
What is the purpose of a literature review in the research process?
Answer: A literature review helps researchers understand existing work, prepare
their arguments, and identify research gaps and questions.
How does a critical literature review help in the research process?
A critical literature review assesses the strengths and weaknesses of existing
studies, compares results, and helps formulate specific research questions.
Research Design
What is the primary consideration when designing a research project?
The primary consideration is determining what type of evidence is needed to
answer the research question convincingly.
What are the main types of research design mentioned in the text?
The main types of research design mentioned are etic vs. emic, quantitative vs.
qualitative, experimental vs. non-experimental, longitudinal vs. non-longitudinal,
and case study vs. group study.
What distinguishes an etic study from an emic study?
An etic study is comparative, while an emic study explores patterns and meanings
in situ.
How does quantitative research differ from qualitative research?

Applied Linguistics prioritizes Descriptive Linguistics over Prescriptive Linguistics. Assess the implications of this preference on language analysis and practical applications in real-world scenarios. Support your evaluation with relevant examples.. " Explain your stance in 170-200 words.
In the field of Applied Linguistics, the emphasis on Descriptive Linguistics over Prescriptive Linguistics carries significant implications for language analysis and practical applications in various real-world scenarios.

    1. Language Variation and Diversity:
 - Descriptive Linguistics focuses on studying how language is actually used by speakers in different contexts and communities. This approach acknowledges and embraces language variation and diversity, which is crucial in multicultural societies. For instance, understanding regional dialects or variations in spoken language within a community helps in effective communication and inclusivity.

    2. Effective Communication Strategies:
 - Descriptive Linguistics prioritizes understanding the communicative intent behind language use. This understanding is invaluable in fields like marketing, where comprehension of how language influences consumer behavior is crucial. For example, companies might use linguistics insights to craft advertising campaigns that resonate with diverse audiences based on their linguistic preferences.

    3. Language Teaching and Learning:
 - In language education, a descriptive approach allows for a more organic and comprehensive understanding of how languages function. Rather than enforcing strict rules, educators can help learners understand the context and pragmatic use of language. This approach aids in language acquisition as learners grasp not only grammar rules but also how language adapts in various situations.

    4. Legal and Forensic Linguistics:
 - In legal settings, descriptive linguistics is vital for understanding language nuances in forensic linguistics. Analyzing language use in legal documents, courtroom interactions, or forensic evidence requires an understanding of how language is naturally employed, not just following prescribed rules. For instance, forensic linguists might analyze language patterns in written threats to identify the author based on their unique linguistic markers.

    5. Computational Linguistics and Technology:
Descriptive Linguistics plays a crucial role in developing language technologies. Natural language processing (NLP) systems, like virtual assistants or machine translation tools, rely on understanding how language is used naturally to function accurately. For instance, Google's algorithms for search and translation are based on large-scale descriptive analyses of language use on the internet.

In contrast, Prescriptive Linguistics tends to establish and enforce standard rules for language use. While this approach might offer stability and consistency in some contexts (like formal writing or certain academic disciplines), it often ignores the natural evolution and diversity of languages. It can hinder effective communication in real-world, dynamic settings where language is fluid and context-dependent.

The preference for Descriptive Linguistics in Applied Linguistics allows for a more nuanced understanding of language as a living, evolving entity, catering to the practical needs of diverse language users across various contexts.

                                    LANGUAGE IN SOCIETY
Topic-035: Language and Society
It is the descriptive study of the effect of any and all aspects of society, including cultural norms,
expectations, and context, on the way language is used, and the effects of language use on society.
Sociolinguistics differs from sociology of language in that the focus of sociolinguistics is the effect
of the society on the language, while the sociology of language focuses on language's effect on the
society.
Sociolinguistics overlaps to a considerable degree with pragmatics. It is historically closely related
to linguistic anthropology and the distinction recently.
It also studies how language varieties differ between groups separated by certain social variables,
e.g., ethnicity, religion, status, gender, level of education, age, etc., and how creation and
adherence to these rules is used to categorize individuals in social or socioeconomic classes. As
the usage of a language varies from place to place, language usage also varies among social classes,
and these sociolects are studied in sociolinguistics.
Linguistic structure and/or behavior may either influence or determine social structure. This is the
view that is behind the Whorfian hypothesis. The claim that the structure of a language influences
how its speakers view the world is today most usually associated with the linguist E.Sapir and his
studentB.L.Whorf. However, it can be traced back to others, particularly to W. vonHumboldt.
Today the claim usually referred to as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis or the Whorfian hypothesis.
Sapir acknowledged the close relationship between language and culture maintaining that they
were inextricably related so that you could not understand or appreciate the one without knowledge
of the other. “Human beings do not live in the objective world alone or alone in the world of social
activity as ordinarily understood, but are very much at the mercy of the particular language which
has become the medium of expression for their society. It is quite an illusion to imagine that one
adjusts to reality essentially without the use of language and that language is merely an incidental
means of solving specific problems of communication or reflection.
The fact of the matter is that “the real world” is to a large extent unconsciously built up on the
language habits of the of the group… ''Words carrying them a myriad possibilities for connecting
us to other human beings.'' (Duranti)
In short, language and society have strong influence on each other. Both are part and parcel of
each other so we cannot strongly oppose the influence of one on another.
Topic-036: Language Diversity and Contact
Linguistic diversity is an inherently enabling condition to its speakers and humankind—a resource
to be protected and promoted—as each language is the repository of immense knowledge built
over centuries of development and use. Linguistic diversity is unevenly distributed across
populations and regions.
Topic-037: Language and Gender
Sex Versus Gender: Sex refers to biological differences while gender refers to the cultural
construction of male and female characteristics.

“The ways members of the two sexes are perceived, evaluated and expected to behave.” (what
different cultures make of sex.)
Gender Boundaries: We demand that the categories of male and female be discrete. Since gender
is culturally constructed the boundaries are conceptual rather than physical. The boundaries are
dynamic, e.g. now it is acceptable for men to wear earrings. Boundaries require markers to indicate
gender such as: Voice Physique Dress Behaviour Hair style Kinetics Language
use
Gender roles: These are asks and activities a culture assigns to the sexes – expected ways of
behaving based on society’s definition of masculine and feminine
Gender stereotypes: Oversimplified but strongly held ideas of the characteristics of men and
women.
 Gender stratification: An unequal distribution of rewards (socially valued resources, power,
prestige, and personal freedom) between men and women, reflecting their different positions in
social hierarchy – a division in society where all members are hierarchically ranked according to
gender
Gender ideology: A system of thoughts and values that legitimizes sex roles, statuses and
customary behavior.
Genderlects: Men often use socially disfavored variants of sociolinguistic variables while women
tend to avoid these in favor of socially more favored variants.
